name: Autosomal Recessive Inheritance Risk
seoDesc: For a recessive condition, risk depends on whether each parent carries one copy. Free autosomal recessive inheritance risk calculator: enter your values and g
summary:
For a recessive condition, risk depends on whether each parent carries one copy. It returns chance of an affected child, chance of a carrier child, chance of an unaffected child and population risk from carrier frequency, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator covers the four standard matings — carrier × carrier, carrier × affected, affected × affected and carrier × non-carrier — and gives the chance for an affected child, an unaffected child and a carrier child. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Autosomal Recessive Inheritance Risk
sections.html:

sections.title: How do I use the Autosomal Recessive Inheritance Risk?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: parent 1 genotype set to Aa — carrier, parent 2 genotype set to Aa — carrier, population carrier frequency of 0.04.

Substituting them into the formula gives chance of an affected child of 25%, chance of a carrier child of 50%, chance of an unaffected child of 25%, population risk from carrier frequency of 0.04%.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Every child of two carriers has the same 25% risk regardless of what happened to earlier children; the dice are independent.

  • Consanguineous couples are more likely to both be carriers, which is why recessive conditions cluster in populations with limited gene flow.

  • Carrier frequency comes from Hardy–Weinberg: 2pq, which for a rare allele is close to 2q.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Multiplying the parents' risks together instead of working from their genotypes.
  • Reading 25% as 'one in four of our children' rather than a per-child probability.
  • Confusing a carrier with an affected individual.

faq.q: If both parents are carriers, why can a child be unaffected?
faq.a: Because there is a 75% chance the child inherits at least one normal allele.

faq.q: What is the risk if one parent is affected and one is a carrier?
faq.a: 50% affected, 50% carrier, none completely free of the allele.

faq.q: What does the Autosomal Recessive Inheritance Risk actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns chance of an affected child, chance of a carrier child, chance of an unaffected child and population risk from carrier frequency. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
